Introduction

What is biochemistry? Britannica defines it as “[the] study of the chemical substances and processes that occur in plants, animals, and microorganisms and of the changes they undergo during development and life”. (https://www.britannica.com/science/biochemistry). A century’s worth of study in biochemistry reveals a core truth embedded in this definition. The processes that occur in plants, animals, and microorganisms are similar to one another. This concept is called the unity of biochemistry and simply states that organisms are quite uniform at the molecular level.

As the great Jacques Monod's said in 1954: "Anything found to be true of E. coli must also be true of elephants!”

In broad terms, all organisms on Earth (and on the space station) must use a limited set of organic and inorganic compounds to build and sustain life. Do you recall what organic and inorganic molecules are?

Organic compounds contain carbon bound to hydrogen. Inorganic compounds may contain carbon bound to other elements.

Organisms rely primarily on hydrogen, oxygen, and carbon – in other words, we are carbon-based life forms that require water to survive. Other elements such as calcium, chloride, potassium, sodium, and magnesium contribute to biomolecular structure and cellular process. You will visit this concept multiple times in many of your courses.

Why does carbon form the basis for life on Earth? Carbon is stable, forming four covalent bonds. Carbon’s strength is, quite literally, it’s strength. This is important for two reasons. First, a carbon backbone can build much larger molecules. Second, breaking carbon-carbon bonds releases more energy, making it an efficient fuel. As a side benefit, after combustion carbon-based molecules form water-soluble carbon dioxide gas. Therefore, the carbon can be reused by the same organism or circulate to a different organism.
Chemical compositions as percentage of total number of atoms.

So, most organisms on Earth rely on large carbon-based molecules, or biomolecules, to build their structure, provide fuel, and live their best life. Classes of Biomolecules

Organisms build a massive array of biomolecules, but these can be classified into only four categories: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. This section outlines the building block, structure, and general roles of each one.

Carbohydrates

Click on the three hotspots in the image to learn more.

• Mono- and Disaccharides

    Simple carbohydrates include monosaccharides (mono – one and saccharide – sugar) such as glucose, fructose, and galactose, and disaccharides (di – two) such as sucrose, lactose, and maltose. Two monosaccharides linked together form a disaccharide. For example, sucrose, or table sugar, is comprised of one molecule of glucose and one molecule of fructose.

  • Carbohydrates

    Carbohydrates, especially glucose, are the main fuel source for most organisms. They consist of carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen atoms and are usually in a ring conformation. We classify carbohydrates into simple and complex carbohydrates.

    Correlate: You’ve probably heard the terms simple and complex carbs in reference to the benefit of complex carbohydrates in grain-based foods. Complex carbohydrates take longer to digest due to their complex structure.

  • Complex Carbohydrates

    In biochemistry, complex carbohydrates are called polysaccharides (poly – many). Polysaccharides are made of hundreds or thousands of monosaccharides linked via glycosidic bonds to form long branching chains. We store the monosaccharide glucose in the form of the polysaccharide glycogen, while plants store glucose as starch. Glycogen is later broken down back to glucose for energy. We will visit glucose and glycogen metabolism in depth in module 4. Polysaccharides have other crucial roles besides storing energy. Highly branched carbohydrate chains also provide structural support, aid in cell identification, and facilitate cell-to-cell interactions.

Lipids

Click on the four hotspots in the photo to learn more.

• Lipids

    Lipids are unique among the biomolecules in that they are not formed from repeating units. Lipids are primarily built from carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen atoms. All lipids in the human body are amphipathic, containing a hydrophilic, or water-loving, head and a hydrophobic, or water-avoiding, tail. We use three types of lipids: triglycerides, phospholipids, and steroids.

    Note: We will cover fatty acid metabolism as well as lipid synthesis in more detail in module 5.

  • Triglycerides

    Triglycerides (fatty acids) contain a hydrophilic glycerol backbone to which three hydrophobic fatty acids are attached via ester bonds. Triglycerides are so named because of the three acyl-bound fatty acids attached to the glycerol backbone. These lipids form our stored fat, or adipose tissue. The fatty acids may be saturated, with no double bonds between carbons or unsaturated, with one or more double bonds. Unsaturated fatty acids are usually liquid at room temperature and include oils such as olive oil and canola oil. Saturated fatty acids are usually solid at room temperature and include fats such as butter or animal fat in meat.

    Notice in the image below the one glycerol attached to three fatty acid chains via their acyl groups. In this example, one FA is saturated and two are unsaturated. The one in the middle contains a single double bond, making it a monounsaturated fatty acid. You may have heard that monounsaturated fats are considered "good" fats. They can be found in nuts and avocados and help fight viceral fat!

  • Phospholipids

    Phospholipids are similar in structure to triglycerides and come in two forms. Diglycerides are formed from two fatty acids, one saturated and one unsaturated, attached to a glycerol backbone, with a modified phosphate group attached to the third carbon. The glycerol molecule combined with the modified phosphate forms the hydrophilic “head” of the phospholipid, and the fatty acids form the hydrophobic “tail”. The other type of phospholipid is a sphingolipid. It contains a sphingosine backbone rather than a glycerol backbone and is often studded with carbohydrates. Phospholipids form the bilayer membranes of our cells and organelles. The hydrophilic heads orient to face the environment, while the hydrophobic tails form the core. The bilayer is highly selective due to the amphipathic properties of the phospholipids. The saturated fatty acid provides structural stability, while the unsaturated fatty acid provides the fluidity required to allow passage of molecules in and out of the cell.

    Notice in the image below how the phospholipids naturally arrange themselves tail to tail, blocking the hydrophobic fatty acids from aqueous environments. This is how they form lipid bilayers! Add in cholesterol and proteins ((see below), and you get a functioning cell membrane!

  • Steroids

    Finally, we have steroids and waxes. Steroids consist of a core structure of four fused hydrocarbon rings with unique R groups. Cholesterol is the most abundant steroid. It intercalates into the lipid bilayer, providing structural support. It is also the precursor for bile salts which aid in fat digestion, and steroid hormones such as the sex steroids testosterone and estradiol, and the stress steroid cortisol.

    While we will not be focusing on waxes in this course, they are important for water retention in plants and protection of the inner ear.

Proteins

Proteins are constructed from amino acids. Amino acids are primarily built from carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, and hydrogen atoms. They contain an amino (-NH3) group, a carboxyl group (-COOH) and an R group (-R) which is unique to each amino acid. Amino acids are linked via peptide bonds to form a long unbranched chain. Human cells use 20 common amino acids, plus 2 rare ones that aren't covered in this course, to build proteins. Amino acids are grouped according to their various properties - polar vs. nonpolar, aliphatic vs. aromatic, acidic vs. basic, and hydroxylic, amidic, or sulfur-containing - which are determined by their R group, as well as whether they are essential, must be consumed or non-essential, can be synthesized in the body. You can see a simple summary of the classification and groupings in the image above, and then more details on each grouping below.

Note: For this class, you will need to know which amino acids fall into which groups. You will not need to know the individual structures. If you plan to take the MCAT, you will need to know some structures, classification, both abbreviations, and the special characteristics. Reach out if you want some help prepping for this area of the MCAT.

Note: Different sources will group different amino acids in different categories, epecially a few special ones like Glycine and Cysteine. We are going with the the way your book groups them.

Click on the four hotspots in the image to learn more.

• Aliphatic Amino Acids

    Aliphatic amino acids have open chain R-group structures. The aliphatic amino acids are: Alanine (Ala), Glycine (Gly), Isoleucine (Iso), Leucine (Leu), Proline (Pro), and Valine (Val).*

    Something special to note about Proline is that it actually an imino acid, not an amino acid; that is, it contains at NH (imino group) when all others contain an NH2 (amino group).

    Those with a solid circle around them are non-essential. Those with a broken circle around them are essential.

    *All of the aliphatic amino acids are non-polar and therefore hydrophobic. The exception is glycine, which is considered hydrophilic despite being non-polar. More on this in module 6.

  • Aromatic Amino Acids

    Aromatic amino acids have R-group structures that form a ring(s). The aromatic amino acids are: Phenylalanine (Phe), Tryptophan (Trp), and Tyrosine (Tyr).*

    Those with a solid circle around them are non-essential. Those with a broken circle around them are essential.

    *Phenylalanine and Tryptophan are also nonpolar, and therefore hydrophobic. Tyrosine is polar, but only weakly interacts with water, so it is considered polar hydrophobic.

  • Electrically Charged Amino Acids

    Aspartic Acid (Asp) and Glutamic Acid (Glu) have R-group structures that are acidic at a neutral pH. These are also known as negatively charged AAs.

    Arginine (Arg), Histidine (His), and Lysine (ys) have R-group structures that are basic at a neutral pH. These are also known as positively charged AAs.

    Those with a solid circle around them are non-essential. Those with a broken circle around them are essential.

  • Hydroxylic, Amidic, and Sulfur-Containing Amino Acids

    Hydroxylic Amino Acids, Serine (Ser) and Threonine (Thr), have R-group structures that contain reactive hydroxyl (OH) groups.

    Amidic Amino Acids, Asparagine (Asn) and Glutamine (Gln), have R-group structures that contain an amide (CO=NH2) group.

    *All hydroxylic and amidic amino acids are polar hydrophilic amino acids.

    Sulfur-containing Amino Acids, Cysteine (Cys) and Methionine (Met), have R-group structures that contain Sulfur (S).

    *The sulfer containing amino acids are split: Methionine is non-polar and hydrophobic, while cysteine is polar and hydrophilic.

    Those with a solid circle around them are non-essential. Those with a broken circle around them are essential.

Proteins are our workhorse. They facilitate cell processes, travel between cells to send communications, receive communications, carry oxygen, provide structure, protect against foreign objects, allow cell mobility… we could keep going. Arguably the most important proteins are enzymes, which catalyze, or enhance, the rate of chemical reactions. We will learn more about enzymes in module 2.

Nucleic Acids

Nucleic acids consist of two macromolecules with which you are likely familiar – deoxyribonucleic acid or DNA, and ribonucleic acid or RNA. Nucleic acids are constructed from nucleotides, a 5-carbon sugar attached to a heterocyclic ring and at least one phosphate group. Nucleotides are linked via a phosphodiester bond to form nucleic acids.

Click on the two hotspots in the image to learn more.

• DNA

    Nucleotides with a deoxyribose sugar base form DNA. These include adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G), and cytosine (C). Notice there is no Uracil (U) in DNA.

  • RNA

    Nucleotides with a ribose sugar base form RNA. These include adenine (A), uracil (U), guanine (G), and cytosine (C). Notice there is no thymine (T) in RNA.
All our genetic information is stored in DNA and transferred to RNA to make proteins. We will review this process later in this module and dive into nucleic acid recycling in module 7.

Learning Objectives

  1. Review the anatomy of a eukaryotic cell.

  2. Define selective permeability, cytoskeleton, organelle, lumen, transport vesicle, endocytosis, exocytosis, and phagocytosis.

  3. Describe the structure and function of the plasma membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondrion, rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosome, and peroxisome.

  4. Explain how cells use endosomes, lysosomes, and secretory vesicles to ingest, digest, and excrete compounds.

  5. Outline the flow of genetic information.

  6. Identify metabolic processes that occur in the cytosol, mitochondrion, smooth endoplasmic reticulum, lysosome, and peroxisome.

Introduction

A cell is generally considered the basic unit of life. It must contain a lipid bilayer membrane that separates the intracellular and extracellular components, creating an intracellular environment different from the extracellular environment. Unicellular organisms include bacteria, archaea, protozoa, yeast (fungi), and some algae. Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes which lack membrane-bound organelles, including a nucleus. Eukaryotes include protozoa, yeast, algae, and all multicellular organisms on Earth. Eukaryotic cells contain their genetic material in a membrane-bound nucleus and have membrane-bound organelles.

FUN FACT: Notice viruses are not on this list. Although the definition of “alive” is still debatable, viruses do not meet all the characteristics of living things. They do not grow, make their own energy, or reproduce on their own.

Let’s review the parts of human cells that we will apply in this course. This is information you have covered more than once before, so it will be skimmed through just to refresh you memory. If you do not remember the parts of the cell, I suggest you go back and review in more detail.

Organelles

Organelles are membrane-bound subcellular structures that perform specific cellular roles. The nucleus, rough endoplasmic reticulum, and Golgi complex form a network to sort proteins, exchange information and material with the extracellular environment, and respond to signals. The mitochondrion, smooth endoplasmic reticulum, lysosome, and peroxisome play a larger role in metabolic processes.

We will start our discussion with two parts that are not considered organelles because they are not membrane bound subcellular structures, but they are vital for cells none the less: the plasma membrane and the cytoplasm.

Plasma Membrane

The plasma membrane is a lipid bilayer that separates the intracellular and extracellular environment. It is composed of phospholipids, with the hydrophilic head oriented to the aqueous environment and the hydrophobic tails in the middle of the bilayer. Due to this orientation, few molecules can pass through, or diffuse, through the plasma membrane. Therefore, the plasma membrane contains several types of membrane proteins to permit the cell to interact with its environment. Transmembrane proteins generally allow for the passage of select molecules, such as glucose and sodium ions. These proteins create a plasma membrane with selective permeability. Other membrane-associated proteins have a variety of roles, including relaying signals in and out of the cell, anchoring the cell, or serving as cellular markers.

Click on the four hotspots in the image to learn more.

• It's a lipid bilayer

    What is a lipid BI-layer? Why it's two layers of lipids! They stack together like a sandwich. As we discussed in the last lesson, the hydrophobic tails hide on the inside together with the hydrophobic heads facing outwards.

  • Cholesterol

    Remember cholesterol from the last lesson? It helps to maintain the fluidity of the membrane by providing stable barriers. As the temperature increases and the phospholipids become more loose/fluid, they cannot move beyond these barriers, keeping the membrane intact. Likewise, as the temperature drops and the lipids begin to solidify and consolidate together, they cannot compact through these cholesterol barriers, maintaining the function of the membrane.

  • Integral Proteins

    Integral, or transmembrane, proteins span through the membrane. They become channels to allow passage of molecules. The membrane is selectively permeable because it only allows certain items to go in and/or out.

  • Peripheral proteins

    Other proteins sit on the surface (inner or outer) of the membrane and serve various functions, from marking of cell types to communcation and anchoring between cells.
Cytoplasm and Cytoskeleton

The cytoplasm is the aqueous intracellular environment. It is crisscrossed by an intracellular skeleton, or cytoskeleton. The cytoskeleton supports the cellular structure, anchors organelles, and is used as a highway network to shuttle molecules around the cell. In the image above, the cytoplasm is green and the cytoskeleton is red. The video at the end of this section has a great visual of the cytoskeleton in action.

Metabolic processes that occur in the cytoplasm include the initial degradation of glucose (glycolysis), and synthesis of glycogen (glycogenesis), fatty acids, amino acids, and nucleic acids. Some steps of glucose synthesis (gluconeogenesis) and glycogen degradation (glycogenolysis) also occur in the cytoplasm.

Now let's check out the rest of the cell

Click on the seven hot spots in the image to review the parts of the cell.

• The Nucleus

    The nucleus is a double lipid-bilayer organelle housing the macromolecules that contain our genetic information – DNA and RNA, composed of nucleic acid biomolecules. Genes that code for proteins reside in our DNA. These genes are transcribed to RNA, which is then transported to the cytosol. Since nucleic acid synthesis occurs in the cytosol, they must be transported from the cytosol to the nucleus for DNA and RNA synthesis.

    Notice the pores around the surface of the nucleus? Those allow the movement of molecules into and out of the nucleus.

  • Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum (RER)

    The RER is so called because the cytosolic side of the membrane is studded with ribosomes. These are protein complexes that translate RNA into proteins comprised of amino acids. As the protein is synthesized, it is guided through pores in the membrane to enter the lumen, or interior of the RER. The new protein is correctly folded, modified if necessary, and sent to the Golgi complex in a transport vesicle, a small sac with a lipid bilayer membrane that sequesters a small amount of cytoplasm and intracellular molecules.

    Quick Note: Not all proteins are synthesized on the RER. Proteins destined for the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes, the plasma membrane, or secretion are synthesized on bound ribosomes. Proteins destined for the cytosol, nucleus, mitochondria, or peroxisomes are synthesized on free ribosomes in the cytosol.

  • Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum (SER)

    The SER is similar in structure to the RER, lacking ribosomes. The SER serves as an excellent place for lipid (triacylglycerol, phospholipid, and steroid) synthesis due to its large plasma membrane providing extensive hydrophobic surface area. Fatty acids are shuttled into the hydrophobic core of the SER membrane, where they are linked to glycerol to form triacylglycerol or phospholipids. Cholesterol and steroid hormones are also synthesized in this hydrophobic core. Cells that carry out extensive lipid synthesis such as adipocytes, Leydig cells of the testis, and hepatocytes in the liver have prominent SER. We will return to these pathways in module 5.

  • The Golgi Body

    The Golgi body, aka golgi complex, aka golgi apparatus, further modifies new proteins and sorts them into transport vesicles depending on their destination. Notice them pinching off in the image? These turn into transport vesicles that will move proteins or other cellular contents outside the cell. Check out the section below to learn more!

  • Lysosomes

    Lysosomes are digestive vesicles, breaking down all four types of biomolecules. You can think of lysosomes as your cell’s digestive system and recycling center. The Golgi complex forms a vesicle containing lysosome-specific enzymes that catalyze, or facilitate, breakdown of macromolecules. The vesicle then fuses with an endosome to form a lysosome. Lysosomes can fuse with phagosomes to destroy bacteria or recycle contents from ageing cells. Cells also use lysosomes to recycle their own contents, a process called autophagy. In this process, a damaged organelle is encased in a lipid bilayer membrane from the ER, then fuses with a lysosome. The free fatty acids, amino acids, monosaccharides, and nucleic acids released by the lysosome can serve as building blocks for biomolecule synthesis or used as fuel. Since lysosomes contain non-specific enzymes that only break down biomolecules to their respective constituents, the only metabolic pathway that occurs in lysosomes is glycogen degradation (glycogenolysis) which we will discuss in Module 4.

    Fun Fact: Similar to your brain telling you it’s time to eat when it senses decreased nutrients, lysosomes can stimulate autophagy when they sense low levels of amino acids.

  • Peroxisomes

    Peroxisomes are specialized vesicles that participate in both breakdown and synthesis of biomolecular building blocks. They form by budding from the smooth endoplasmic reticulum in a similar manner to lysosomes budding from the Golgi complex. Metabolic processes relevant to this course that occur in the peroxisome include initial degradation of very long fatty acids (β-oxidation) and certain amino acids. Other processes include breakdown of reactive oxygen species such as hydrogen peroxide, synthesis of the omega-3 docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), and synthesis of bile acids that aid digestion.

  • Mitochondria

    Ah, the “powerhouse of the cell” (can you feel my eyes rolling as I say that?)! Mitochondria produce about 90% of the energy we use. These little bundles of energy are thought to be prokaryotes that formed an endosymbiotic relationship with a eukaryotic cell about 1.5 billion years ago. Like many prokaryotes, mitochondria have a circular DNA, no organelles, and unique ribosomes. They divide by fission independently of the eukaryotic cell. Therefore, high-energy tissues such as skeletal muscle contain more mitochondria per cell, and increased energy demands (such as exercise) can increase the number of mitochondria.

    Mitochondria have an outer and inner membrane separated by an intermembrane space. The inside of mitochondria is called the matrix. The inner membrane has multiple invaginations into the matrix called cristae. Cristae increase the surface area on which metabolic reactions can take place. The central hub of metabolism, the citric acid cycle, occurs in the mitochondrial matrix. Breakdown of fatty acids (β-oxidation) also occurs in the matrix. Oxidative phosphorylation is the end step of glucose metabolism and takes place on the inner membrane. We will discuss the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation in Module 3, and breakdown of fatty acids in module 5.

Cellular Transport

Special transport vesicles called secretory vesicles transport proteins or other cellular contents outside the cell. The process by which the secretory vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane to expel its contents is called exocytosis. The Golgi complex also receives transport vesicles from the plasma membrane called endosomes, via endocytosis. Endocytosis allows for cellular uptake of necessary biochemicals and cellular response to signals. A unique type of endocytosis called phagocytosis is the engulfing of large amounts of extracellular material forming a phagosome. This process is used by certain white blood cells to destroy bacteria and by our own cells to recycle contents from ageing cells. The final steps of sphingolipid synthesis occurs in the Golgi complex.

Click on the two hotspots in the image to learn more about exo- and endocytosis.

• Exocytosis

    Exocytosis in the process by which items are removed from the cell. Molecules and waste are put into secretory vesicles, shown here originating as part of the golgi body, and then they fuse with the cell membrane to release the contents. This same process is how new parts of the cell membrane are created and cell receptors are placed on the membrane surface.

  • Endocytosis

    Endocytosis is the process by which items are brought into the cell.

    Phagocytosis is known as cell eating because it is for engulfing larger particles.

    Pinocytosis is known as cell drinking because it is for taking in small particules suspended in extracelluar fluid

    Cells communicate with each other and can take vesicles for uptake through cell-mediated endocytosis.

Introduction

We discussed the importance of carbon as a backbone for our biomolecules in lesson 1. Despite this crucial role, it is weak forces that that lend structure and function to the cell and its processes. What are weak forces? Why and how are they beneficial? Many weak interactions give a significant amount of stability to large structures. Additionally, weak forces are transient, meaning a cell can dynamically interact with its environment. Without transient interactions, life would not exist as we know it. These weak forces are dependent on the properties of water.

Vocabulary Review

Before we discuss the properties of water, let’s make sure we remember polarity and charge by reviewing some quick flash cards.

  1. CHARGED MOLECULE (AKA: ION)

    Show answer

    A molecule with a net electrical charge due to an uneven number of electrons to protons. The charged particle is negative when it gains electron(s) from another atom. The charged particle is positive when it loses electron(s) to another atom.

    Reminder: Two atoms that have transferred an electron between them share an IONIC BOND.

  2. UNCHARGED MOLECULE

    Show answer

    A molecule with an overall zero net charge due to an equal number of protons and electrons.

  3. POLAR MOLECULE (AKA: DIPOLE)

    Show answer

    A molecule with an overall zero net charge, but electric charge distributed asymmetrically about its structure, resulting in a partial positive end and a partial negative end. This results from uneven sharing of electrons

  4. NONPOLAR MOLECULE

    Show answer

    A molecule with an overall zero net charge and electric charge distributed symmetrically about its structure, resulting in no net charge on any ends of the molecule.

Thanks for taking time to review. Examples of charged molecules are sodium ions (Na+) and chloride ions (Cl-). Uncharged molecules may be polar or non-polar. Polar molecules have areas of slight positive or negative charge due to unequal electron sharing within a covalent bond.

Water

What makes water special? Water is known as the solvent of life. It lubricates the environment, allowing for the random movement of chemicals. Through this random movement, molecules can interact – proteins bind substrates, plasma membranes are stable and fluid, fuel is burned for energy. In past biology courses, you likely covered a variety of properties of water that make it essential to life. Let's refresh ourselves on those very quickly.

NOTE: As you watch the following video, pay special attention to time 0:45-2:25 as we will discuss this further.
Properties of WaterOpen on YouTube

As you should have noticed, the video outlined two major propoerties of water vital for biochemical processes, both of which happen to account for the other properties that make water so valuable for life:

First, water molecules form dipoles; that is, water is polar. Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen, meaning the shared electrons of the O-H covalent bond spend more time around oxygen. Thus, the oxygen has a partial negative charge (𝛿-), and the hydrogens have a partial positive charge (𝛿+), called a permanent dipole.

The interaction of a polar water molecule with a polar or charged biomolecule allows biomolecules to dissolve in water. Thus, polar and charged molecules are hydrophilic. In contrast, nonpolar molecules are hydrophobic; because they lack charged atoms, they cannot dissolve in water. Instead, nonpolar molecules cluster together like a drop of oil. Living systems take advantage of this hydrophobic effect to form 3D biomolecular structures.

Second, water forms hydrogen bonds, a type of weak bond that forms between a 𝛿+ hydrogen and partial or fully negatively charged atoms of other molecules. Each 𝛿+ hydrogen of one water molecule can form a hydrogen bond with the 𝛿- oxygen of another water molecule. Have you ever dropped water drops onto a penny until a water dome formed, observed the U-shaped meniscus at the water’s surface in a graduated cylinder, or watched a bug walk across a river? As discussed in the video, all these phenomena are due to the cohesive property of water. Hydrogen bonds are common among biomolecules and lend stability to folded proteins, the hydrophilic head of phospholipids, and DNA/RNA helix structures.

Weak Interactions

Covalent bonds are the strong bonds that bind atoms into molecules. As previously mentioned, water is made of polar covalent bonds. There are also ionic bonds that form molecules by passing electrons, like we see in sodium chloride. These are called intramolecular forces because they form within molecules.

But it is the "weak", noncovalent forces - which can either be attractive or repulsive - that allow the biochemical interactions necessary for life to take place. These are intermolecular forces, occurring between molecules. They are dependent on distance between atoms and differ in their configuration and strength. A key factor of weak forces is their reversibility. In this section, we will dive into the three major types of weak molecular forces: Dipole Interactions, Hydrogen Bonds, and van der Waals interactions.

NOTE: We are a biochemistry group, so we call a specific kind of interaction a van der Waals force. For us, it is the dispersion forces explained in the video.
Intermolecular ForcesOpen on YouTube

Dipole Interactions

Dipole interactions are electrostatic interactions between oppositely charged groups within or between biomolecules. These can be ion-dipoles (AKA salt bridges), in which an ion is attracted to the oppositely charged end of a polar molecule, or dipole-dipole, in which one charged end of a polar molecule is attracted to the oppositely charged end of another polar molecule. Dipole interactions are the reason salt can dissociate in water.

Salt bridges are important for binding of charged molecules and ions in amino acid interactions for protein folding as well as in the bonding between proteins and DNA.
Hydrogen Bonds
Hydrogen BondsOpen on YouTube

As mentioned earlier, hydrogens acquire a slight positive charge when covalently bound to an electronegative atom. When in liquid form, dipole bonds are constantly forming between a 𝛿+ hydrogen and a 𝛿- atom of another molecule. When the element bonding with water is nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine, the bond is especially strong, and is known as a hydrogen bond. This is because these elements are the most electronegative, meaning the attraction, or pull of the hydrogen end of the water molecule to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine is stronger than most, creating a tight dipole-dipole interaction.

Hydrogen bonds form between water molecules, giving water its cohesive properties. Although hydrogen bonds are strong in terms of dipole interactions, they are quite weak in terms of "bonds", making them transient in nature; in liquid water, hydrogen bonds are constantly forming and breaking as the molecules flow and bump into each other. Yet, hydrogen bonds are required for appropriate folding and interaction of biomolecules. Hydrogen bonds keep DNA in its double-stranded shape and allow for strand dissociation during DNA replication. Hydrogen bonds also keep proteins in their proper shape. We will revisit this concept often throughout the course.
Check out this 50 sec video of hydrogen bonds in water
van der Waals Interactions

van der Waals interactions are similar to dipole interactions in that they occur due the attraction between partial positive and negative charges. In fact, dipole interactions are a specific type of van der Waals interaction, as mentioned in the video. Unlike other dipole interactions, van der Waals interactions can occur between ALL molecules, even non-polar ones!

Just as molecules are constantly moving, the subatomic particules within molecules are constantly moving as well, and there are many times the electrons around any one atom are situated asymmetrically. This creates a transient area of partial charge around that atom and a complementary asymmetry of partial charge around neighboring atoms of another molecule, thus creating an opportunity for a moment of attraction between these two. This also explains how you can have an ion-induced dipole interaction.

These forces act over a very short distance, and the strength of the attraction varies with distance, as seen in the chart above. Interestingly, if the distance is too close, reaching what is known as the van der Waals contact distance (a term I would know if I were you), the attraction is counteracted by the repelling forces of the electron clouds.

These forces are the weakest individual intermolecular forces; however, they have a cumulative effect that can be substantial (i.e. together they are strong), especially in the cases of macromolecules such as DNA and proteins that have atoms in close proximity to each other.

An example of the additive effect of van der Walls forces is a gecko walking up a wall or across a ceiling.

Hydrophobic Effect

Despite the importance of the interactions between water and partial or full electrical charges, some fully hydrophobic biomolecules cannot interact with water. Think of shaking a container with oil and water. The oil forms into droplets separate from the water. This is the hydrophobic effect, or the tendency of nonpolar compounds to self-associate in an aqueous environment.. This is not due to any bonding or interaction between the molecule in the oil, but rather due to the minimization of the disruption to the interactions between the water molecules around the oil.

The second law of thermodynamics says that a spontaneous process will increase the entropy, or the randomness, of a system. Water molecules are forced to form a “cage” around a single hydrophobic molecule. When two hydrophobic molecules come together, some of the water molecules forming the “cages” are freed into solution. Thus, hydrophobic molecules don’t associate because of attraction or affinity. They simply associate because it excludes water and increases the entropy of the system. This is a crucial difference between the hydrophobic effect and weak interactions. Weak interactions occur due to attraction or affinity.

The hydrophobic effect drives organization of lipids and proteins. Amphipathic phospholipids form lipid bilayers, with the hydrophilic head forming hydrogen bonds with water and the hydrophobic effect forcing water from the hydrophobic tails. Hydrophobic amino acids in a protein associate together in the protein core via the hydrophobic effect, surrounded by polar or charged amino acids that can interact with water and each other.

Introduction

We have been emphasizing the value of transient and reversible interactions/reactions in biochemistry. The last lesson focused on interactions occuring due to electron sharing, pulling, donating, and accepting. In this lesson, we are going to look at another interaction-donating or accepting a proton, also called a hydrogen ion or H+. The hydrogen ions within a solution are used to delineat the solution as an acid or a base. Acids donate H+ while bases accept H+. The pH of a solution is determined by the concentration of hydrogen ions…. Or is it?

No doubt you learned the previous concept in chemistry before. However, recall that our biochemical reactions occur in water, which is polar. This means that for any free H+ found in solution, there is just as likely to be an H+ bound to electronegative oxygen atoms in water via a dipole-dipole interaction, thus forming: H3O+.

H+ + H2O ↔ H3O+

Therefore, when we say pH is determined by measuring the concentration of protons, hydrogen ions, or H+, we could also mean the concentration of hydronium ions or H3O+. All these terms are used interchangeably.

pH ranges from 0-14 with 7 as neutral. pH below 7 is acidic, while pH above 7 is basic. pH is tightly regulated in living systems because a change in pH affects weak bonds. This makes sense; weak bonds are electrostatic interactions, dependent on difference in charge. Therefore, a change in the number of positive or negative ions in the solution can disrupt them. In this lesson we will review acids and bases, calculate pH, relate ionic strength to biological interactions, and discuss one system by which we maintain pH.
This will help you remember what an acid is
This will help you remember what a base is
Acids and Bases and Water, Oh My!
Acids, Bases, and WaterOpen on YouTube

Recall that acids are proton donors and bases are proton acceptors. Organic acids predominate in biomolecules. Acids ionize to form a hydrogen ion and its conjugate base. Conversely, a base that accepts a proton forms its conjugate acid.

Acid ↔ H+ + conjugate base

Base + H+ ↔ conjugate acid

Another way to write this is: HA ↔ H+ + A- Where HA is the acid, and A- is the base.

The conjugate base is named after the acid plus the suffix -ate. For example, lactic acid and lactate are a conjugated acid-base pair. Most organic acids at physiologic pH of 7.4 (the standard pH of human blood) are in conjugate base form, so you will see these terms more often (for example, pyruvate instead of pyruvic acid).

One minor, but important property of water we didn't discuss in the previous lesson is its tendency to dissociate; water has a slight ability ionize, forming a hydronium ion (proton/H+) and hydroxide ion (OH-).

H2O + H2O ↔ H3O+ + OH-

For simplicity’s sake, we can rewrite the equation as:

H2O ↔ H+ + OH-

The amount of water that dissociates is so small that it can be negated when discussing pH. However, the ability of water to form hydronium and hydroxide ions allows it to act as both an acid and a base, an important property required for biochemical interactions.

Equilibrium Constant

The equilibrium constant (also known as the dissocation constant) is the point at which a reversible reaction is at equilibrium. In other words, products on both sides of the reaction are being made at such a rate that the overall concentration of each doesn’t change. It is calculated using the ratio of the molar concentrations of the reactants and products.

[H+][A−]
Keq=
[HA]

Let’s return to water as our example. Since hydronium and hydroxide ions continuously recombine to form water molecules, an individual hydrogen or oxygen cannot be stated to be present as an ion or as part of a water molecule. At one instant it is an ion; an instant later it is part of a water molecule. Individual ions or molecules are therefore not considered. We refer instead to the probability that at any instant in time a given hydrogen will be present as an ion or as part of a water molecule. We are describing the ionization of water statistically using the equilibrium constant for the dissociation of water.

Remember the formula, modifying for water:

[H+][OH-]
Keq=
[H2O]

So, what do we know? (PS- We know this because I'm telling you. I don't expect you to know this off the top of your head.)

  • The molarity of pure water is 55.5M
  • The probability that a hydrogen (and therefore a hydroxide) ion in pure water will exist is 1.8 x 10^-9 (which calculates out to 1x10^-7M).

Now we can plug and play.

[1x10^-7M][1x10^-7M]
Keq=
[55.5M]

Solve for Keq, remembering to cancel out the units where appropriate, and we end up with Keq = 1.8x^10-16mol/L.

As you can see, the denominator (concentration of water) is quite large compared to the numerator (concentration of ions multiplied), giving a very small Keq.

What did this teach us? Since Keq is a ratio, reactions that favor the reactant will have a Keq less than 1, while reactions that favor the products will have a Keq greater than 1.

Apply this to our lesson and we get: Strong acids and bases produce a significant number of protons or hydroxide ions and have a Keq >>1, significantly shifting the pH.

Important Note: Although we can find Keq experimentally, in practice we look up these values on reference tables. Therefore, while I will want you to know what the equilibrium constant is, how to calculate it, and how to interpret one if I provide it, it is unlikely I will make you calculate it on a test.

One last thing to take into the next section:

The fact that the concentration of water is so large compared to the concentration of ions multiplied reiterates what we mentioned earlier: the dissociation of water is very slight, and is therefore negligible. The molarity of water is too great to be significantly affected by dissociation, and is therefore considered constant. We therefore create a new constant specific for water called the ion product using just the numerator.

Kw = [H+][OH-]

Kw always equals 10^-14(mol/L)^2 for all aqueous solutions. Notice the 14 in there? This is why the pH scale goes up to 14!

In a nutshell, what you need to know is that pH and pOH add up to 14. So if pH is 4, pOH must be 10. This is an example of an acid, as we will see in the next section.
pH and pOH
pH definitionOpen on YouTube

pH stands for potential hydrogen and is calculated using the concentration of hydronium ions/ proton/H+. It’s a way to linearly represent logarithmic changes in proton concentration. The example below demonstrates that the pH of pure water is 7.

pH=−log[H+]

pH = -log (1x10^-7) = 7

NOTE: All logs are base 10, so a 1 unit change in pH is equivalent to a 10 fold change in concentration.

pOH is the same calculation, substituting [ OH-] for [H+]. Meaning, pOH=−log[OH-]

Let's take a quick look at how pH and pOH are related in this short video.
pH and pOHOpen on YouTube

pOH is not used often in biochemistry; however, it is important to understand that OH- ions are associated with bases because the OH- can accept a H+. The higher the concentration of OH- ions, the stronger the base.

As we mentioned previously, pH+pOH =14. Therefore, we can easily find both the pH and the pOH if given either [ OH-] or [H+].

Henderson-Hasselback Equation

We know acids donate a proton and bases accept a proton. We also know that strong acids are more likely to donate protons and strong bases are more likely to accept protons. But how can we determine if something is a strong acid? In other words, how do we know to what extent a substance will donate a proton? The strength of the acid is determined by how likely it will dissociate. Remember, if it is likely to dissociate, that means it will break into its ions more readily, therefore freeing up the H+ ions to be donated.

We are therefore going to start with the equation for calculating dissociation (aka equilibrium) constant in evaluating how strong of an acid something is. Spoiler alert: Ultimately, we are going to end up with a new equation, known as the Henderson-Hasselback Equation, which is used to describe the behavior of weak acids and buffers. So, let's see how we get there:

Replacing water with a generic acid in the equilibrium constant formula gives us the following:

HA ↔ H+ + A-

[H+][A−]
Ka=
[HA]

Quick Note: Notice we used Ka here. The equilibrium constant for any reversible reaction is denoted Keq and for acid-base reactions it’s denoted Ka.

You are often going to see a new term pKa moving forward. This is going to be our measurement for how weak or strong an acid is. Let's take a look.

Strong acids such as hydrochloric acid (HCl) fully dissociate. 0.1M HCl produces ~0.1 M H+ and a pH of 1.0. The Ka of HCl is ~1.3x106.

However, biological systems rarely use strong acids. Our blood pH is tightly controlled at 7.4 and perturbing the system can result in severe illness or death. Weak acids that predominate in biological systems, such as acetic acid, remain partially protonated, meaning they only partially dissociate. In other words, they are weak acids. To what extent a weak acid remains protonated depends on the pH of the environment. The Henderson-Hasselback equation below illustrates this concept.

[A−]
pH= pKa + log
[HA]

The pKa is the pH at which half of the acid is dissociated (because log (1) =0). For example, if the pKa = 7, at a pH of 7, the acid will exist as equal parts acid and conjugate base.

If pH is above the pKa, [A-] is dominant (so it is existing in the deprotonated conjugate base form, meaning it is a stronger acid - aka weak base - because it donated its protons) and if pH is below the pKa, [HA] is dominant (so it is existing in the protonated conjugate acid form, meaning it is a weaker acid - aka a base - because it has accepted protons). If pH is equal to the pKa, then it's a great buffer (more on buffers below) because it is existing as about equal parts of each. If an acid has more than one hydrogen capable of dissociating, each hydrogen has its own pKa, noted as pKa1, pKa2, etc.

Want to know a sneaky trick? pKa = log (Ka)

Wait, that's not simply put at all?!!! You're right. Here's it is in a nutshell:

pKa is a number that shows how weak or strong an acid is. More precisely – pKa is the negative log base ten of the Ka value (acid dissociation constant). It measures the strength of an acid — how tightly a proton is held by an acid. The lower the value of pKa, the stronger the acid and the greater its ability to donate its protons. . A strong acid will have a pKa of less than zero.

Now, let's walk through a problem together.

The pKa of aspirin is 3.5. Calculate the [A-] / [HA] ratio at physiologic pH 7.4

  1. Write the equation: 7.4 = 3.5 + log ([A-] / [HA])

  2. Subtract: (7.4-3.5) = log ([A-] / [HA])

    1. 3.9= log ([A-] / [HA])

  3. Raise each side by the log base. 10^3.9 = [A-] / [HA]

    1. 7943=[A-] / [HA]

Most important part, what does this mean?

  • There are approximately 7943 A- molecules in aspirin for every one HA.

But what does THAT mean?

  • It doesn't have a lot of HA around. It has a TON of A- around. A- is the conjugate base. It isn't a very good acid. There doesn't seem to be any protons available to donate, but lots of negative ions ready to accept free protons.

Show answer

Did you get that question right? It seemed tough, right? Well, let's break it down. We already talked about all of it.

We said earlier If pH is above the pKa, [A-] > [HA] and if pH is below the pKa, [HA] > [A-]. We also said pKa of aspirin is 3.5.

In the stomach, pH of 1.5 is below pKa, so HA, the acid, is greater. In the small intestines, pH of 3.5 is equal to pKa, so the small intestine is the scenario with more base available for absorption.

Why does all this matter?

The ionization of an individual molecule can affect absorption, metabolism, solubility, weak bonding properties, or activity. Aspirin is only absorbed as its conjugate base. Ionized forms of acids and bases are more polar and thus more soluble in water, but also have a harder time diffusing through the hydrophobic core of the plasma membrane. Loss of H+ in deoxyribonucleic acids (DNA) destroys their hydrogen bonding capabilities, destabilizing the DNA double helix. Loss or gain of H+ in amino acids affects the electrostatic charge and can cause protein misfolding. Therefore, pH must be maintained, and molecules must be in their conjugate acid or base form or convert between them as appropriate.

That brings us to arguably the most important biochemical role of weak acids and their conjugate bases… buffering the system from pH changes.
Buffers
BuffersOpen on YouTube

A buffer is a conjugate acid-base pair that resists significant changes in pH. In biological systems, buffers predominantly neutralize hydrogen ions. The best buffers are a combination of a weak acid or base and its conjugate.

Important Note: One of the most common misconceptions is that buffers neutralize solutions. This is incorrect. Buffers maintain pH, regardless of what the pH is!

One of our most important biological buffers is the bicarbonate buffer system. It maintains blood pH at 7.4 and facilitates transport of carbon dioxide gas (CO2) to the lungs. CO2 is a byproduct of glucose combustion; the average person produces almost 2.5 pounds a day! CO2 reacts with water to produce carbonic acid (H2CO3), a weak acid. Carbonic acid dissociates to form a proton and its conjugate base bicarbonate (H+ + HCO3-).

CO2 + H2O ↔ H2CO3 ↔ H+ + HCO3-

The pKa1 of carbonic acid is 6.1 at body temperature (37°C). Using Henderson-Hasselback, we can calculate the ratio of bicarbonate to carbonic acid (you should try this on your own).

7.4 = 6.1 + log(x)

10^(7.4-6.1) = x

20 = x

So, there is a 20:1 ratio of bicarbonate to carbonic acid in our bloodstream. This produces sufficient bicarbonate to buffer excess protons from other organic acids such as lactic acid produced during exercise. In the lung, enzymes favor the reverse reaction, producing CO2 for exhalation and preventing excessive acid build-up in the bloodstream.

What do you think would happen to your blood pH if your breathing rates were to change? This would alter the amount of CO2 available and push the above reaction to the left or the right, depending on if we were increasing or decreasing respiration. This is a question I am going to leave here for you to ponder and discuss together.

QUICK NOTE: A buffer solution resists changes in pH most effectively at pH values close to the pKa of the solution. For any given conjugate acid-base pair, the pH buffering capacity is estimated as pKa ± 1. Intuitively this makes sense. The pKa is the pH at which half of the acid is dissociated, maximizing the range at which changes in [A-] or [HA] minimally impact the pH. This is demonstrated in the image below.
